introduction: Margaret arrives in England as Henry VI's queen, accompanied by a peace agreement that has cost England valuable French territories. The marriage intensifies conflict among nobles who already resent Gloucester's authority as Protector. His wife Eleanor's ambitions offer his enemies an opening, while York privately measures his own claim to the throne. Beyond the court, grievances over government, privilege and defeat in France make the commons increasingly volatile. Henry hopes for justice and peace, but competing ambitions steadily narrow his freedom to act.

fullSynopsis.text: Henry welcomes Margaret and rewards Suffolk, who has married her by proxy. Gloucester protests the loss of Maine and Anjou and the absence of a dowry. Margaret, Suffolk, the Cardinal and other nobles unite against him, despite ambitions that divide them. York outwardly supports Gloucester while privately planning to claim the crown. Eleanor, Gloucester's wife, dreams of becoming queen and hires practitioners to question a spirit. Hume, secretly paid by Suffolk and the Cardinal to entrap her, assists. The spirit gives obscure predictions about Henry, Suffolk and Somerset before York and Buckingham interrupt the ceremony and arrest its participants.

Gloucester exposes Simpcox's pretended miraculous recovery of sight and mobility, but news of Eleanor's arrest brings his own humiliation. Henry sentences her to public penance and banishment on the Isle of Man, orders punishments for the conjurers and requires Gloucester to surrender his Protector's staff. Gloucester refuses to rescue his wife unlawfully and trusts his innocence to protect him, despite her warning that enemies will destroy him. Separately, Peter defeats his drunken master Horner in a judicial combat over alleged treason; dying, Horner confesses. York explains his dynastic claim to Salisbury and Warwick, who pledge allegiance while he counsels secrecy.

At Bury, Gloucester is arrested on charges he denies, including misuse of soldiers' pay. Henry believes him innocent but fails to protect him. After the king leaves, Margaret, Suffolk, the Cardinal and York agree that Gloucester should die. York receives command against Irish rebels and privately plans to use his new army for his own advancement. He has recruited Jack Cade to stir English rebellion under the name Mortimer and test popular support for York. Murderers then report Gloucester's death to Suffolk, confirming his orders. Suffolk announces the death as a discovery, and Warwick's examination of the body supports suspicion of murder.

The commons demand Suffolk's death or exile. Henry banishes him despite Margaret's pleas, and their intimate farewell reveals their attachment. The Cardinal dies terrified and delirious, speaking of Gloucester and judgment, while Henry prays for mercy. At sea, Suffolk is captured by men who denounce his part in England's losses and Gloucester's destruction. His rank and defiance cannot save him. Walter Whitmore takes him away and returns with his severed head, giving a grim turn to the earlier prediction that he would die by water. Margaret subsequently appears mourning over the head as rebellion approaches London.

Cade claims noble descent as Mortimer, though his companions' asides mock the story. He promises cheap food, common property and an end to money, while ordering a clerk hanged for literacy. His followers defeat and kill the Stafford brothers, enter London and defeat its defenders. Henry withdraws to Kenilworth. Cade assumes authority, orders records burned and condemns Lord Saye, whose defense of his public service cannot move him to mercy. Saye and his son-in-law are beheaded, and their heads are displayed together. The movement's claims of liberation become accompanied by arbitrary killing and Cade's demands for personal dominion.

Buckingham and Clifford offer pardon and invoke Henry V's victories, winning Cade's wavering followers back to the king. Cade flees. Hungry and isolated, he enters Alexander Iden's garden, challenges its owner and is killed in combat. Iden brings the head to Henry and is knighted. Meanwhile York returns from Ireland with an army, publicly demanding Somerset's removal while intending to seize the crown. He dismisses his soldiers when Buckingham assures him Somerset is imprisoned. Seeing Somerset free beside Margaret, he abandons concealment and declares his claim openly. His sons, Salisbury and Warwick support him, and the opposing nobles prepare for battle.

At Saint Albans, York kills old Clifford, and Richard kills Somerset beneath the Castle Inn's sign, which Richard identifies as fulfillment of the warning to avoid castles. Young Clifford finds his father's body and vows pitiless revenge against the York family, including its children. Margaret and he urge Henry to flee the defeated field. York and his allies reunite with the surviving Salisbury, whom Richard has repeatedly rescued. Their victory leaves Henry alive and still a rival; Salisbury warns that merely putting their enemies to flight is insufficient. They resolve to pursue the king toward London before parliamentary summonses go out.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: Henry receives Margaret as his queen and makes Suffolk a duke, but Gloucester and other nobles resent the peace's surrender of Maine and Anjou. Suffolk, Margaret, the Cardinal, Buckingham and Somerset seek Gloucester's fall for differing reasons. York secretly hopes to turn their divisions toward his own claim to the crown. Eleanor urges her husband toward ambition, which he rejects, and arranges a conjuration through Hume. Hume has been paid by her enemies to encourage this dangerous undertaking. At court Margaret tears petitioners' requests and strikes Eleanor, while Peter's charge against Horner raises questions about York's title and leads to an ordered judicial combat. Eleanor's spirit ceremony produces ambiguous prophecies before York and Buckingham break in and arrest the participants.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: Gloucester and the Cardinal's hostility continues during the royal hawking party. Gloucester exposes Simpcox's false claims of a miraculous cure, then receives news of Eleanor's arrest. York privately sets out his hereditary claim to Salisbury and Warwick, gaining their allegiance while urging patience until Gloucester's enemies have weakened the government. Henry condemns the conjurers and sentences Eleanor to penance and banishment. He also ends Gloucester's protectorship. In the judicial combat, Peter unexpectedly overcomes Horner, whose friends have made him drunk; Horner confesses treason before dying. Gloucester watches Eleanor's public humiliation but refuses to break the law to free her. She warns him of the conspiracy against his life, while he insists that loyalty and innocence will keep him safe.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: At Parliament in Bury, Gloucester's opponents accuse him of treason and financial misconduct. He denies the charges, and Henry declares his trust but allows the arrest. Margaret, Suffolk, the Cardinal and York agree to have Gloucester killed. York is sent with troops against Irish rebellion, privately welcoming an army for his own designs and describing Cade as his agent in England. Murderers report to Suffolk that his command has been executed. Henry grieves when Gloucester's death is announced, and Warwick identifies signs of violence on the body. The commons' demands bring Suffolk's banishment. Margaret and Suffolk part in anguish, revealing their attachment. The Cardinal then dies in terror, while Henry refuses to endorse Warwick's judgment of his soul.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: Suffolk's sea captors reject his rank and ransom, and Walter Whitmore beheads him. Margaret mourns over his head as Cade's rebellion advances. Cade claims the Mortimer lineage and promises radical reform, but orders punishment for learning and exercises violent personal authority. His men kill the Staffords, take London and defeat the city's forces. Henry withdraws as Cade orders destruction of records and the deaths of Lord Saye and his son-in-law. Buckingham and Clifford reverse the crowd's allegiance with pardon and appeals to Henry V's memory. Henry pardons the returning rebels, but learns that York is approaching with an army. Cade, abandoned and starving, fights Iden after entering his garden and is killed, ending the rebellion's leadership.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: York comes from Ireland intending to claim the crown but tells Buckingham that his army seeks only Somerset's removal. Assured that Somerset is imprisoned, he disperses his troops and offers loyalty. Henry meanwhile knights Iden for bringing Cade's head. Somerset's free appearance with Margaret provokes York to assert his royal claim openly. Edward, Richard, Salisbury and Warwick stand with him, while Clifford remains loyal to Henry. In the battle at Saint Albans, York kills Clifford and Richard kills Somerset beneath the Castle Inn's sign. Young Clifford vows merciless revenge on the York family and helps urge Henry's flight. The victorious Yorkists greet Salisbury's survival, then decide to pursue the king toward London; the crown has not yet changed hands.
